summary:
Yucatán operates an administrative route to legal gender recognition. A 2024 reform to the state's Civil Registry Law, published in the Diario Oficial of 26 April 2024, created a procedure through which transgender people can update legal gender on identity documents without a court order. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state rundown of March 2025 records Yucatán on that basis, and the procedure is what a trans visitor's document situation turns on when entering or being stopped in the state.

Yucatán sits within the majority of Mexican states that have legislated recognition. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had enacted a legal gender-recognition procedure by that date, and named six states whose legislatures had enacted none. Yucatán is among the 22, not the six. The same reporting warns that implementation differs sharply between states, so a valid document in Yucatán does not guarantee smooth handling elsewhere in Mexico.

Yucatán stands under Mexico's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal across the country since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. Same-sex acts have been decriminalised federally since 1871. At federal level the Chamber of Deputies passed a conversion-therapy ban in March 2023 by 267 votes to 104, following a 69 to 16 Senate vote in October 2022.

Partnership recognition in Yucatán arrived through the courts before the legislature. On 1 July 2013 the Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled that two petitioners were able to marry, and the first same-sex couple in the state married legally on 8 August 2013. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015, and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022.

Yucatán is listed as enacting a conversion-therapy ban on 25 August 2021, in force alongside the state ban from Mexico City of 31 July 2020 and bans in other states. The federal conversion-therapy legislation noted above remains the national layer of that protection.

Formal law sits well ahead of enforcement in Mexico. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many states now run administrative recognition procedures while calling on those without one to adopt them. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation; the organisation's report of 6 March 2024 found that delays and refusals in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, with knock-on effects in banking, health care and dealings with police.

Violence against trans people in Mexico is documented at scale. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. At least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of 2024, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the twelve months to mid-2024. Mexico City's Congress approved the Paola Buenrostro law in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP of 22 November 2024 concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.
tangentialFactors:
Sexual diversity is documented as tolerated among Yucatán Maya groups, a cultural observation rather than a legal protection the state enforces on a visitor's behalf.

The sequence of Yucatán's marriage equality — court orders in 2013, appellate dismissals in 2015, constitutional amendment in 2021, secondary legislation in 2022 — follows the wider Mexican pattern in which litigation outran statute for roughly a decade before legislatures caught up. Legal gender recognition followed a similar path nationally, with administrative procedures appearing state by state through 2024 and 2025.

Yucatán's conversion-therapy ban of 25 August 2021 sits among a growing set of state bans, including Mexico City's of 31 July 2020, and alongside the federal ban passed by the Chamber of Deputies in March 2023. Coverage therefore depends on where a person is physically located at the time.

Impunity for killings of trans people is the recurrent regional context. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights warned in 2024 that impunity may have reached alarming levels, and the Paola Buenrostro law of July 2024 exists because the 2016 murder it is named for was never punished.
localsOnly:
Yucatán residents update legal gender through the administrative procedure created by the 2024 Civil Registry Law reform rather than through litigation, which removes the court-order step that residents of the six states with no procedure still face.

Residents of Yucatán have had access to same-sex marriage since the first couple married on 8 August 2013, with the route regularised by the Congress of Yucatán's constitutional amendment of 7 September 2021 and the secondary-legislation amendment of 1 March 2022.

Conversion therapy is prohibited in Yucatán under the listing of 25 August 2021, and federally under the ban the Chamber of Deputies passed in March 2023 by 267 to 104 after the Senate's 69 to 16 vote of October 2022.

Residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity report practical consequences in banking, health care and dealings with police; the administrative procedure exists precisely to end that mismatch, but the enforcement gap identified by Caroline Beer's November 2024 analysis applies to Yucatán as to other states.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state processing times, fees, residency requirements or documentation thresholds for Yucatán's administrative gender-recognition procedure, so the practical burden on a visitor or new resident is unresolved.

Whether Yucatán's Civil Registry officials apply the 2024 procedure uniformly across municipalities, and whether any refusing official has been sanctioned, is not sourced here.

The six states named by Human Rights Watch on 31 March 2025 as having enacted no recognition procedure are not identified in this inventory, so the distance between Yucatán and the weakest jurisdictions in Mexico cannot be specified.

No source in this inventory records killings of trans people specifically in Yucatán, nor any conviction under the state's conversion-therapy ban; both remain not sourced.

Human Rights Watch warned in March 2025 that implementation of recognition procedures varies from state to state, but the inventory gives no state-level account of how Yucatán's procedure performs against that warning.
